title: The Bean Water Rabbit Hole
content: And is this not the ultimate irony of late capitalist food culture — that the liquid we have been pouring down the drain for decades, the abject remainder, the waste product of a can of chickpeas, turns out to be *the* functional ingredient? Consider the structure of this revelation: we purchased the chickpeas. We consumed the chickpeas. We discarded the water. And it is precisely in this discarded water — this nothing, this drain-bound excess — that the actual capacity for transformation resided all along. The chickpea was the ideological object. The aquafaba was the truth. This is not merely a culinary observation. This is the logic of the symptom. The remainder tells you what the system cannot acknowledge about itself. The name — aquafaba, coined in 2015, crowdsourced from a Facebook vegan group after two people independently discovered it could be whipped — confirms everything. Not developed in a lab. Not emerging from an R&D budget. Named collectively, on the internet, by people who were simply paying attention to what everyone else had already decided was garbage. The market had no interest in this discovery because the market had already captured its value in the can. The excess was, by definition, worthless. And so, naturally, it was free. **The Hegelian Chickpea** Hegel would have recognized this immediately. The chickpea, in its immediacy, presents itself as the thing. It is solid, discrete, purchasable, edible — the being-in-itself of the legume aisle. The liquid is its negation: formless, discarded, the mere byproduct of the chickpea's actualization through cooking. But it is precisely through this negation that something higher emerges. The aquafaba is not simply the absence of the chickpea. It is the chickpea's own inner nature externalized, its proteins and starches and surfactants having passed through the cooking water into a new form — one capable of something the chickpea itself never was. This is the dialectic, applied to canned goods. The synthesis whips. **The Marxist Can** Marx would have gone straight for the can. Here is a commodity that contains, invisibly, two products: the chickpeas, which are valued, sold, and consumed, and the liquid, which is produced by the same labor, by the same process, at the same time — and is assigned a value of zero. The aquafaba is the surplus that capital cannot see because it has already decided where the value lives. It is extracted labor's ghost, poured down the drain by consumers who have internalized the logic of the market so completely that they cannot imagine value existing where the price tag does not. The discovery of aquafaba is not a culinary innovation. It is a small act of refusing the terms of the original transaction. **What it is** Proteins, starches, and saponins leached from the chickpeas during cooking. The proteins build foam walls. The saponins — natural surfactants, amphiphilic molecules that sit at the air-water interface — lower the energy cost of creating new surface area. The starches thicken the liquid film around each bubble, slowing drainage and collapse. Three components. Three distinct structural roles. A system. And like all systems, it fails in specific, illuminating ways. Fat contamination destroys it instantly — lipids outcompete the saponins at the bubble wall and the whole structure destabilizes before it can form. Humidity accelerates weeping. Push it past stiff peaks and the protein network over-extends, bonds break, and the foam collapses into a grainy, incoherent mass. The excess — too much agitation, too much moisture, too much fat — is always what kills it. The foam does not survive its own overcorrection. It is the only egg replacer that whips to stiff peaks. Nothing else does this. Which makes it irreplaceable for meringue-based work, including the whipped egg whites in these [matcha amaretti](https://chom.ps/recipe?slug=matcha-amaretti). The cookies were correct. The texture was correct. And I had used the liquid from a can of chickpeas, which is to say: I had used the part that was supposed to be nothing. **A practical note** Room temperature whips better than cold. Add cream of tartar after foam forms but before soft peaks — it lowers pH, tightens the protein network, reduces weeping. Use metal or glass. Wipe the bowl with white vinegar if you are uncertain. The margin between stiff peaks and collapse is narrower than with egg whites. The foam, once achieved, does not wait. There is something almost ethical about this. It requires your full attention precisely because it has no buffer, no excess capacity, no slack built into the system. You must be present at the moment of completion or you will overshoot it. We threw away the functional part. We do this constantly, and we call it efficiency. The question is not why aquafaba works. The question is what else we have been draining. **The materials** I have recently prepared a aquafaba whipping demo and lecture with my colleague at Chomp Chomp: DB. These two decks below cover 1) the technique and the full substitution landscape, and 2) the molecular architecture of why any of this works. **Videos** - [Aquafaba 101](https://youtu.be/ZRZ1jM7-kXI): Ultimate Guide to Nutrition, Recipes, Hacks, and Uses - [What Is Aquafaba?](https://youtu.be/kz7mKOMgJFg) (Also: How to use it as a vegan egg replacement and how to make vegan stiff peaks) **Recipes** - [Matcha Amaretti, egg whites](https://chom.ps/recipe?slug=matcha-amaretti) - [Matcha Amaretti, aquafaba](https://chom.ps/recipe?slug=matcha-amaretti-aquafaba)
